chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ibn Faddal, from the one who mentioned him, from al-Tayyar, who said:

Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said to me: 'Which thing do you deal in? Which thing do you make?' So I said, 'I am not involved in anything.' He said: 'Then take a place, sweep its yard, sprinkle water on it, and spread out your merchandise therein. When you do that, you will have fulfilled what is obligated upon you.' He (the narrator) said: 'I went and did it, and I was granted provision.'

key_terms.بَيْتاً: a shop/place of trade — in classical Arabic, 'bayt' could refer to a room or space for business
key_terms.بِسَاطاً: a mat or spread on which goods are displayed for sale; metaphorically, one's entire commercial enterprise
key_terms.رُزِقْتُ: I was granted provision/livelihood — the passive form emphasizes that God is the ultimate provider of sustenance
key_terms.فِنَاءً: the yard or front area of a shop/house, the space maintained to attract customers
key_terms.وَجَبَ: was obligated/required — the use of this root indicates a religious duty, not merely a recommendation

ai.seo_question: What did Imam al-Baqir say about a Muslim's duty to seek livelihood and work?
ai.summary: Imam al-Baqir (AS) counseled a companion named al-Tayyar who was idle and uninvolved in any trade or work. The Imam's instruction — to take a shop, prepare it with care (sweeping, watering, displaying goods) — reflects the Shia teaching that human effort and practical preparation are the believer's religious duty, while sustenance (rizq) ultimately comes from God. This hadith was addressed to a specific companion who perhaps felt his inaction was spiritually acceptable, and the Imam corrected this by linking worldly effort to religious obligation.
